title: RPS Says the US Healthcare Liability Market 'Isn't Broken but It's Starting to Bend': Hospital Capacity Falls to $5 Million Lines, Some Pricing Doubles and Abuse Cover Is Disappearing
summary: Risk Placement Services' 2026 US Healthcare Market Outlook, summarised by Risk & Insurance on June 17, 2026, says healthcare liability capacity is contracting, with hospital lines of $5 million now typical instead of $20 million, some pricing doubling, abuse limits being dropped from hospital policies and carriers cutting limits for human and social services.
description:
Risk Placement Services, RPS, a US wholesale insurance broker, has published its 2026 US Healthcare Market Outlook Report, and the trade publication Risk & Insurance summarised it on June 17, 2026. The findings below come from that summary. The RPS report itself was not reviewed. The Risk & Insurance page also carried a sponsored piece from another company; that content is produced separately, its figures are attributed to other sources, and this article does not use it. The summary does not address retentions, which are the amounts insureds pay before insurance responds, or nuclear verdicts, so this article does not either.

The overall picture

RPS describes a market under structural stress: capacity is contracting, placements take longer and pricing is sharply higher. Demand for cover keeps growing, but capacity, especially in the upper layers of insurance towers, keeps shrinking. A tower is a layered program in which several insurers each provide a slice of cover above the one below. RPS says the market has not broken, a phrase echoed in the title of its outlook, which describes a market that is bending and not breaking. Hospital programs that once closed in days now take weeks, and some placement pricing has doubled year over year.

Smaller lines and higher prices

The report says the era in which one carrier provided $20 million on a hospital program is over. The common maximum is now $5 million. A calculation made here shows that a $50 million tower at $5 million per carrier needs at least 10 carriers, which matches the report's statement that such a tower may need 10 or more. On price, Margaret Jacobs of RPS is quoted as saying pricing has risen from about $10,000 per $1 million of coverage to $20,000 or more in some states. At those rates, a million dollars of cover costing $20,000 means a 2% rate on line, a ratio of premium to limit calculated here.

Hospitals and abuse coverage

Markets no longer routinely include abuse limits in hospital liability policies. Insureds respond by building what the report calls split towers: they buy as much abuse limit as is available and complete the rest of the program without it. James McNitt of RPS says he does not expect this to turn around anytime soon. For a hospital, a split tower means that part of its liability protection excludes abuse claims, and so the organisation carries that risk itself or buys a smaller amount.

Physicians

Shared-limit programs, in which all physicians in a group draw on one aggregate limit, are replacing separate-limit programs. This reduces the carrier's exposure but creates gaps for the group, since one large claim can use up the limit for everyone, which increases demand for physician excess coverage. RPS reports rising claim severity in obstetrics, gynecology, neurosurgery and pediatrics, and warns that some admitted carriers and risk retention groups are underpricing that business. It adds that more than 71% of physicians use telemedicine at least weekly, and that the risks it creates are pushing more exposure into the excess and surplus market, where insurers have more freedom on rates and terms.

Human and social services

This segment shows the sharpest cutbacks. Carriers that offered $10 million limits have cut back to $5 million or less, and several program markets have exited. Coverage is shifting from occurrence-based to claims-made. Occurrence cover responds to events that happened during the policy period, whenever the claim is made, while claims-made cover responds only to claims reported during the policy period, and retroactive dates on abuse coverage are advancing. Sublimits on abuse, assault, molestation and self-inflicted injury are increasingly common. RPS warns that these sublimits can make excess coverage effectively worthless after a large claim, since the excess layer may sit above a small sublimit. It also says some nonprofit foster care agencies are uncertain whether they can stay in business.

Residential care

Senior living remains workable for most accounts, according to the summary, though operators that have grown through mergers and acquisitions face closer scrutiny. Behavioral health and human services residential programs are being pushed into the excess and surplus market for the first time.

Submissions and brokers

Submission quality now determines whether accounts get quoted or declined. Carriers weigh broker relationships and track records more heavily; as McNitt put it, carriers are underwriting the broker, not just the risk. For healthcare organisations, that means a complete, well-prepared application and a broker with credibility in the market are part of getting cover.

What to take from it

The report is from a broker with an interest in the market it describes, and its figures are examples given by named RPS staff, not market-wide statistics. It does not give an average price change across the market. Still, the combination of smaller lines, higher prices and dropped abuse cover points to a market where buyers should expect more carriers, higher cost and more negotiation.

Limits

This article relies on a trade-press summary of a broker's report, and its figures are quoted from named individuals. It is general information, not insurance advice.
source_name: Risk & Insurance, summarising the RPS 2026 US Healthcare Market Outlook Report (June 17, 2026)
image_alt: Stethoscope and medical paperwork representing healthcare liability coverage (illustrative)
key_points: RPS says demand keeps growing while capacity, especially in upper tower layers, keeps shrinking, but that the market has not broken; hospital programs that once closed in days now take weeks, and some placement pricing has doubled year over year.

A single carrier providing $20 million on a hospital program is a thing of the past, the common maximum is now $5 million, and a $50 million tower may need 10 or more carriers; pricing has risen from about $10,000 per $1 million of cover to $20,000 or more in some states.
Markets no longer routinely include abuse limits in hospital liability policies, so insureds are building split towers, and RPS does not expect this to reverse soon.

Physician programs are moving to shared limits, severity is rising in obstetrics, gynecology, neurosurgery and pediatrics, and more than 71% of physicians use telemedicine weekly, pushing exposure into the excess and surplus market.

Human and social services carriers have cut $10 million limits to $5 million or less, shifted from occurrence to claims-made cover and added abuse sublimits, while submission quality and broker relationships now decide whether accounts are quoted.
why_it_matters: Hospitals, physicians, care homes and social service agencies need liability cover to operate. When capacity shrinks and prices double, organisations must buy cover from many carriers, accept gaps such as missing abuse limits, and in some cases question whether they can continue.

title: Bank of England's July 2026 Financial Stability Report: Stretched AI-Linked Valuations, Rising Equity-Market Leverage and Frontier-AI Cyber Risk, While the Countercyclical Buffer Stays at 2%
summary: The Bank of England's Financial Policy Committee, in its Financial Stability Report of 7 July 2026, said valuation, sovereign debt and credit vulnerabilities persist, equity-market leverage has risen substantially and frontier AI has raised cyber and operational risks, while judging UK banks well capitalised and keeping the countercyclical capital buffer at 2%.
description:
The Bank of England's Financial Policy Committee (FPC) published its Financial Stability Report on 7 July 2026, alongside the record of its meeting. The report is the committee's regular assessment of risks to the UK financial system and of the resilience of banks and other firms. The previous report was published in December 2025. This article draws on two secondary summaries, published by Regulation Tomorrow and by A&O Shearman, because the full report was not retrieved. The summaries do not include the underlying charts and data, so anyone relying on a specific figure should consult the Bank's report itself. One of the summaries gives the date of the meeting record as 26 June 2025, which conflicts with the July 2026 publication; the other gives 26 June 2026, which this article follows.

The overall judgment

The FPC said the UK financial system has remained resilient and continued to support the real economy. At the same time, it said vulnerabilities in risky asset valuations, sovereign debt and risky credit markets, including private credit, remain and in some cases have become more pronounced since December 2025.

The backdrop

The summary describes a US–Iran memorandum of understanding that has eased near-term pressure, with energy prices and bond yields down from earlier peaks. Volatility and uncertainty persist. The FPC warned that further geopolitical developments could worsen existing vulnerabilities, and that higher leverage in equity markets raises the risk that several vulnerabilities could crystallise at once.

Valuations, concentration and leverage

The committee noted a substantial increase in the use of leverage in equity markets. Equity valuations are more stretched, particularly for AI-related companies, and market concentration has increased. Hedge fund leverage has risen sharply, which the committee said could amplify market shocks. The summaries do not quantify the fall in prices that the FPC considers plausible, and this article does not estimate one.

AI and debt financing

The FPC examined the macro-financial risks of the AI transition across sectors. It noted that AI investment is driving unprecedented demand for debt financing, while uncertainty remains about the profits and productivity gains that will follow. That combination, of heavy borrowing against uncertain returns, is the specific concern the summaries describe.

Private credit and sovereign debt

Risky and private credit markets remain vulnerable because of leverage, liquidity and valuation concerns. On sovereign debt, the committee pointed to rising public debt levels and to leveraged trading strategies as adding to risks.

Cyber and operational resilience

The report says rapid advances in frontier AI since December have significantly increased cyber and operational resilience risks. In the committee's words, "more capable AI systems can identify and exploit vulnerabilities at greater scale." It called for robust resilience frameworks, closer coordination with technology providers and effective implementation of the UK's critical third parties regime, which applies to firms that provide key services to the financial sector.

Households, businesses and banks

The FPC judged households and businesses broadly resilient. Household debt and vulnerability measures remain low by historical standards. Higher energy costs and borrowing rates will increase debt-servicing pressure, particularly for low-income households and for smaller, more leveraged firms that rely on private credit or leveraged loans.

The UK banking system is well capitalised and liquid, according to the summary, and stress tests indicate that it can withstand severe shocks while continuing to lend. The committee stressed the need to manage banks' links with non-bank financial institutions. It maintained the countercyclical capital buffer, the extra capital banks must hold when risks are elevated, at its neutral rate of 2%.

Other policy steps

The committee welcomed the Bank's publication of the stress scenario for the private markets system-wide exploratory scenario (SWES). It expects to use that exercise to assess how banks and non-banks active in private markets would respond to a severe but plausible global downturn. The summaries do not report any results.

Following its review of bank capital requirements, the FPC will work with the Prudential Regulation Authority to simplify and modernise the capital framework. The stated aims are to make buffers more usable and releasable in stress, and leverage ratio requirements more proportionate and effective, while keeping overall resilience. Over the longer term, the authorities support a single releasable capital buffer. Proposed leverage ratio changes include removing the countercyclical leverage buffer, aligning with international standards and increasing the share of leverage buffers that can be released in stress.

The committee also welcomed the Bank's policy statement and consultation on a draft code of practice for systemic sterling-denominated stablecoins, and recent statements by HM Treasury and the Financial Conduct Authority on strengthening money market fund resilience.

What the summaries leave out

The summaries do not provide the report's quantitative scenarios or its estimates of how a market correction might affect UK output. This article therefore gives no figure for the possible effect of a market correction on UK output.
source_name: Bank of England Financial Policy Committee (Financial Stability Report, 7 July 2026), as summarised by Regulation Tomorrow and A&O Shearman
image_alt: Financial charts and data representing systemic risk assessment (illustrative)
key_points: The Financial Stability Report was published on 7 July 2026 and says vulnerabilities in risky asset valuations, sovereign debt and risky credit, including private credit, remain and in some areas are more pronounced than in December 2025.

The FPC noted a substantial increase in the use of leverage in equity markets, stretched equity valuations particularly for AI-related companies, greater market concentration and a sharp rise in hedge fund leverage.

Rapid advances in frontier AI since December have significantly increased cyber and operational resilience risks, because 'more capable AI systems can identify and exploit vulnerabilities at greater scale'.

The committee judged UK households and businesses broadly resilient and banks well capitalised, able to withstand severe stress tests while continuing to lend, and maintained the countercyclical capital buffer at its neutral rate of 2%.

It also welcomed publication of the private markets system-wide exploratory scenario, plans to modernise the bank capital framework, a draft code for systemic sterling stablecoins and moves to strengthen money market funds.
why_it_matters: The Financial Policy Committee's judgments shape capital requirements for UK banks and signal where the central bank sees risks building. For savers, borrowers and investors, the report identifies which parts of the financial system the Bank is watching, from AI-driven market valuations to private credit and cyber resilience.
